I assume you mean tightly around 1? That's where they should be.

>> plotNuse(qamTr,ylim=c(-0.2,0.2))
> Error in boxplot.stats(stdvs/medianSE, ...) :
> unused argument(s) (ylim = c(-0.2, 0.2))

An easy work-around for this is:

z <- plotNuse(qamTr)
plotBoxplotStats(z, ylim=c(.5,2))

I'm unable to recreate these errors below on a local dataset. They
all work fine for me. Here is my complete set of commands from a
fresh R session, as described in the exon array vignette page:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/human-exon-array-analysis

----------------
library(aroma.affymetrix)
cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType(chipType,
tags="coreR3,A20071112,EP")
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName("tissues", cdf=cdf)
setCdf(cs,cdf)

bc <- RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs, tag="coreR2")
csBC <- process(bc,verbose=verbose)

qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)

plmTr <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
fit(plmTr, verbose=verbose)

rs <- calculateResiduals(plmTr, verbose=verbose)
qamTr <- QualityAssessmentModel(plmTr)
plotNuse(qamTr)

z <- plotNuse(qamTr)
plotBoxplotStats(z, ylim=c(.5,2))

plotRle(z)
----------------


Have you fit the probe level model in advance of these commands?
Given that your NUSE values are tightly around 0, I suspect maybe
not. Otherwise, can you give a complete code example, and maybe run
it from a fresh R session and check whether that solves your problem.
And, as usual, if you get an error, the output of traceback() is much
appreciated ... and of course, the output of your sessionInfo().

Hope that helps.

Cheers,
Mark

> Also, what does it mean if the boxplot for a chip's exon-level NUSE
> suggests that this chip maybe an outlier (i.e. the median is higher
> than those of other chips), while its RLE boxplot doesn't suggest that
> (its RLE boxplot align with others)? Should I treat this chip as an
> outlier at all?

The NUSE is generally more sensitive than the RLE, so the NUSE will
often show a problem that the RLE misses.

> Another question I have been puzzled was:
> I noticed that exon-level NUSE boxplots typically show higher
> heterogeneity across chips, while gene-level NUSE boxplots don't. And
> RLE boxplots don't show much heterogeneity either at the exon-level or
> gene-level. Could someone give me an idea about why this is the case,
> and whether I should define an outlier based on the gene-level or exon-
> level NUSE/RLE?

The exon level NUSE will often be larger than the gene-level, and that's
because the NUSE is basically a measure per-gene of how much more
variable the sample is compared with the other samples. With only 4
probes (compared to all probes in a gene), its usually more variability
generally, so the boxplots are bigger. So they aren't really comparable.

Generally I find the gene-level NUSE the one that most frequently finds
the problems. But if there's any real obvious outlier in any of the
plots, then its a possible problem regardless of the other plots.
However, there is always variation and always one sample that will be
the worst, by definition, so make sure it does truly seem like an outlier.

Best,

On Dec 1, 9:39 am, Elizabeth Purdom <epur...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Also, what does it mean if the boxplot for a chip's exon-level NUSE
> > suggests that this chip maybe an outlier (i.e. the median is higher
> > than those of other chips), while its RLE boxplot doesn't suggest that
> > (its RLE boxplot align with others)? Should I treat this chip as an
> > outlier at all?
>
> The NUSE is generally more sensitive than the RLE, so the NUSE will
> often show a problem that the RLE misses.
>
> > Another question I have been puzzled was:
> > I noticed that exon-level NUSE boxplots typically show higher
> > heterogeneity across chips, while gene-level NUSE boxplots don't. And
> > RLE boxplots don't show much heterogeneity either at the exon-level or
> > gene-level. Could someone give me an idea about why this is the case,
> > and whether I should define an outlier based on the gene-level or exon-
> > level NUSE/RLE?
>
> The exon level NUSE will often be larger than the gene-level, and that's
> because the NUSE is basically a measure per-gene of how much more
> variable the sample is compared with the other samples. With only 4
> probes (compared to all probes in a gene), its usually more variability
> generally, so the boxplots are bigger. So they aren't really comparable.
>
> Generally I find the gene-level NUSE the one that most frequently finds
> the problems. But if there's any real obvious outlier in any of the
> plots, then its a possible problem regardless of the other plots.
> However, there is always variation and always one sample that will be
> the worst, by definition, so make sure it does truly seem like an outlier.
>
> Best,
> Elizabeth

session, and run the commands start to finish. There are a couple

plmData/ and probeData/ directories and when you run the commands,
aroma.affymetrix will just recreate them. Alternatively (and more
elegantly?), you can add a 'force=TRUE' argument to all the process()
and fit() commands that you use.

Hope that helps.

Mark
